am=Data$am

wt=mtcars$wt
mpg=mtcars$mpg
cyl=Data$cyl


plot(wt,mpg)


#Estimation of linear model

M1=lm(mpg~wt,data=mtcars)
summary(M1)


lm

We need to studies the mpg with using the 31 variables in dataset

```{r}
Data=mtcars[,-1]

cor(mtcars)

c = cor(cbind(Data), cbind(Data))
c^2
 
```

Visualisation

```{r}
plot(mtcars$disp,mtcars$wt)

Z=lm(disp~wt+hp)
summary(Z)


v=-129.9506+82.1125*wt+0.6578*hp
plot(mtcars$disp,mtcars$hp)

```

D'après le ploting on remarque que les variables wt et disp sont probablement lie et apparenté par une regression linéaire simple

```{r}
#Estimation of linear model

disp=Data$disp
cyl=Data$cyl
M1=lm(disp~wt,data=mtcars)
M2=lm(disp~cyl,data=mtcars)

summary(M1)
summary(M2)
```

```{r}

library(lars)

 X = cbind(1,v,hp,qsec,drat,wt)
 X1 = cbind(1,v,qsec,drat)

 
 
 regLasso = lars(X1, mpg, type = "lasso")
 summary(regLasso)

```

```{r}
coef_step <- coef(regLasso)[4, ] 
coef_step[coef_step != 0]
```

Voila les trois variables qui nous permettront de construire notre regression linéaire multiple

```{r}

# Modèle de régression multiple
#modele <- lm(mpg ~ v+qsec+drat, data = mtcars)
modele <- lm(mpg ~wt+disp+ hp+qsec+drat+wt, data = mtcars)


# Résumé du modèle
summary(modele)

AIC(modele)


```

```{r}
a=step(modele)
```

```{r}
bptest(modele)


#e=mpg-(-4.3978*wt+0.9462*qsec+1.6561*drat)
plot(wt,e)
plot(drat,e)
plot(qsec,e)
```

```{r}
plot(a)
e=residuals(a)
shapiro.test(e)
```
